newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Iliescu front-runner ahead of Romania vote.
newsitem.headline: Iliescu front-runner ahead of Romania vote.

text.p: Romanian voters, still mired in poverty seven years after their bloody revolution, choose this weekend between President Ion Iliescu's policy of cautious change or the risks of faster economic reform.
Opinion polls give Iliescu, a former Communist in power since 1989, a slender lead in Sunday's presidential contest. A run-off will almost certainly be needed later in the month.
Iliescu's Party of Social Democracy (PSDR) trails liberal rivals in a race for parliament which could force the president to work with political foes demanding policy changes.
With campaigning halted on the eve of the poll, newspapers urged Romanians weighed down by low wages, soaring prices and widespread corruption to turn out in force to polling stations.
Some mocked Iliescu's contention that slow reform has saved Romania from social unrest.
"Are things not the other way around? Stability is one thing, stagnation quite another," wrote independent daily Azi.

The government daily Vocea Romaniei said on Saturday Romanians should opt for "change for the common good. Taking turns at running the country is no misfortune, but rather a part of the political rules of democracies."

Seven years after Iliescu took power after dictator Nicolae Ceausescu was ousted and shot, average monthly wages stand at less than $100 -- about a third of levels in Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic.

The International Monetary Fund has suspended credits, complaining of currency controls, continued subsidies to outdated industry and expected annual inflation of 40 percent, well beyond agreed limits.
Residents of Bucharest and other major towns are suspicious of Iliescu, who has been jeered by workers who once backed him. The president's bedrock of support remains the countryside.

Iliescu, who easily won elections in 1990 and 1992, has portrayed himself as a bulwark of stability. He points to the steep economic decline and conflicts in neighbouring Bulgaria and Yugoslavia, as pitfalls to be avoided.

"Romania has achieved profound but cautious change. We have lived modestly but with the certainty of what will happen tomorrow," he told a television debate this week with all 16 presidential candidates.
"Just look at our neighbours. Destructive conflicts have taken place, wages have gone unpaid for months."
His main opponents, academic Emil Constantinescu and former Prime Minister Petre Roman, want to speed up reforms, boost living standards and modernise Romania.

Constantinescu's Democratic Convention (CDR) has drawn up a "contract with Romania" akin to that of the U.S. Republican Party. It pledges to resign if it fails to cut taxes, improve social benefits and modernise rural areas within 200 days.
Roman, prime minister for 22 months after Ceausescu was executed, promises similar reforms to wipe out what he calls the blight of 4.5 million Romanians below the poverty line.
Opposition parties accuse the PDSR of a plan to rig the election after a bitter campaign marred by personal attacks.
Both opposition groupings say they will make no deals with Iliescu's PDSR in coalition talks certain to follow a close outcome. But neither has announced a post-election strategy.
